newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Gambia's Jammeh extends hand to vanquished opposition.
newsitem.headline: Gambia's Jammeh extends hand to vanquished opposition.

text.p: Gambian coup leader Yahya Jammeh, fresh from winning a mandate to continue in office as civilian head of state, called on vanquished civilian opponents to join his government but poured scorn on his main rival.
Lawyer Ousainou Darboe, the strongest of three civilian rivals in Thursday's poll, remained holed up at the Senegalese embassy with two wives and aides for the third day.
"As far as far as I am concerned Mr Darboe is the best person to explain why he is there ," Jammeh said in a Friday night television interview.
"We don't know what he has done that would warrant him to go and seek refuge in a foreign embassy."
Pressed to elaborate, he added: "If you go to the market and someone shouts 'thief' and you start running and someone grabs you; well, you have to explain why you are running."
Local newspapers reported rumours that Darboe and some political associates had received unspecified threats.
Key members of Darboe's United Democratic Party said to be afraid for their lives, were not available for comment.
Jammeh, a 31-year-old U.S.-trained army officer who toppled an elected government in the West African state in 1994, has been anxious to shake off the stigma of a coupmaker.
He was declared winner of the presidential elections to end military rule with 56 percent of the vote, outpolling Darboe by more than 78,000 ballots.
In his first comment on Friday night, Jammeh said he had no problem working with the opposition.
"What is important now is to develop our country for the benefit of our children, not the political party you belong to," he told the local television interviewer.
"Everybody has a right to belong to any party. What is important is whether you've lost or you've won, you have to join the bandwagon for the interest of all Gambians," he added.
Jammeh overthrew the government of Sir Dawda Jawara who had ruled the tiny country of one million people since independence from Britain in 1965.

He resigned from the army last month to contest the elections that he brought forward from 1998 following Western pressure. Western creditors froze aid and some put a temporary ban on their nationals travelling to the tourist haven.

Wild rejoicing greeted the election result with thousands of people in cars, buses and on foot on Friday converging on the city centre in a rare show of exuberance in the sedate majority Moslem nation.
Voting itself was peaceful and orderly, with 88 percent of some 444,000 registered voters casting ballots.
In what could easily be a first in Africa, electoral commission chairman Gabriel Roberts said there had been no petition against the conduct of the election or the results.
However, the legal framework for the poll was slammed by critics at home and abroad as meant to ensure Jammeh's victory.
Jammeh banned Gambia's main political parties and experienced politicians linked to Jawara.
